parts:
I didn't write MCDS, so I can't say for sure but I think your conclusion=20
is unlikely to be correct unless it is for a model with no covariates at=20
all. Otherwise, it
should be computing D=3Dsum i=3D1 to n 1/p_i/(2LW)=3Dsum i=3D1 to n=20
f_i(0)/(2L). If p_i is constant then this will be equivalent to the CDS=20
estimator of nf(0)/(2L).
If you have clustered popn then the estimators are D=3Dsum i=3D1 to n=20
s_i/p_i/(2LW)=3Dsum i=3D1 to n s_i*f_i(0)/(2L), where s_i is size of ith=20
group. You can test if
you want by using mrds with the single observer method. I know that it=20
uses the above in mrds. --jeff

parts:
Jeff;
Thanks for the reply. I tried calculating the abundance estimates in R usi=
ng the formula you specified, with the detection function parameter estimat=
es from the Distance Stats File, and the original observation data, but got=
results that differed by 5-6%. For example, for one particular stratum, I=
got N=3D153 using D=3Dsum i=3D1 to n s_i/p_i/(2LW)=3Dsum i=3D1 to n s_i*f_=
i(0)/(2L), vs. N=3D160 output in Distance. =20

Also puzzling me is why when using MCDS with covariates, Distance prints an=
estimate of f(0) on the Density Estimates summary page (and how is that va=
lue calculated)? The abundance estimates given by Distance match perfectly=
with the value of f(0) reported, using N=3DArea*E(s)*n*f(0)/(2L). =20

I'm left thinking that perhaps when cluster size is not a covariate, MCDS u=
ses covariates to fit the detection function, but then uses the f(0) from t=
hat to calculate density and abundance estimates using the formulas from CD=
S. Can someone please confirm or refute this?
Thanks,
Eric

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: how does MCDS calculate density and abundance when cluster
parts:
Eric, I believe what Distance is doing when cluster size is not selected
as a covariate is to first estimate number of clusters based on
sum(1/p_i), then estimate mean cluster size, and multiply the two. I
think the f(0) reported is the mean estimate for observed clusters. I
don't now recall why we did it that way rather than the method in the
advanced distance sampling book, but it could well be because it is not
consistent to not use cluster size in the detection function, but then
to use a formula that is designed for when detectability depends on
cluster size. I'll see if Len has a better memory than me.

Steve

Eric, list,

I'll add a bit to this but probably Len will have the final word on it.

I believe what Steve says is correct, and Distance gets first the=20
estimated number of clusters based on sum(1/p_i) and then it multiplies=20
this up by an estimate of mean cluster size. And you can even choose to=20
have say a size bias regression estimate for mean cluster size, although=20
that is, similar to what Steve points, another inconsistent approach in=20
the sense that cluster size was apparently not selected as a covariate=20
and so size bias is not expected (Yet I must confess I have done it in=20
the past - but can also add that I would not do it now! Subject for=20
another discussion though...)

Cheers,

Tiago
